title: Submarines: Exploring Under the Sea
summary: How submarines developed from a simple wooden rowing boat into nuclear vessels that explore the deepest parts of the ocean.
poll: Submarines have done more good for science and exploration than harm as weapons of war.

versions.title: Submarines: Exploring Under the Sea
versions.text:
Look at that submarine. It is long. It is gray. Soon it will dive.

Long ago, a man built a boat that could go under water. He lived in England. He used wood and leather. Rowers sat inside and moved it with oars. It could sink down and come back up.

Years went by. A man built a new kind of boat. It was shaped like a shell. One man sat inside. He turned a handle to move it. He used it in a war.

A submarine can sink and float. It takes in water to go down. It pushes the water out to come back up. This lets it dive and rise.

Later, boats like this got a new shape. Navies used them more.

Then a new kind of submarine came. It did not need to come up for a long time. It used a new kind of power.

Today, submarines go deep into the sea. They find old ships. They study strange fish. They help us learn about the deep sea.

Today, submarines can explore deep into the sea. They find old sunken ships. They study strange fish. They help us learn about the deep, dark sea.

versions.title: Submarines: Exploring Under the Sea
versions.text:
Look at a submarine at the dock. Soon it will dive beneath the waves.

Long ago, a man built a boat that could travel under water. He lived in England. He packed it with wood and leather to keep the water out. Rowers sat inside and moved it with long oars. It was used for fun at first. Later, it was used as a weapon in wars.

Years after that, a man tried something new. He built a boat shaped like a turtle shell. He did not use rowers. He turned a hand crank to move it. It proved that a small crew could work.

A submarine works in a simple way. Tanks let water in and the boat sinks down. Air pushes that water back out and the boat rises. As water moves in and out, the submarine dives and floats.

Later, a team built a small, round submarine with a better shape. It surprised the whole world with its new design.

Then a crew rode a submarine deep down. They stayed under for a long time. They were among the first to travel that far below the waves.

Today, some submarines can stay down for months. Crews use them to study the deep sea.

Picture a submarine at its dock, its crew already aboard, waiting to slip beneath the waves at the start of a long voyage.

Long before modern navies, a man in England named Cornelius Drebbel built a boat that could travel beneath the sea, at a time when few people believed such a craft could work. He packed it with wood and tough leather to keep the water out, and rowers inside moved it slowly with long oars. It was tried first for amusement, and later inspired cruder weapons used in European wars.

Years later, an American inventor named David Bushnell envisioned a markedly different design, one meant for a surprise attack unseen beneath the water. He built a small craft shaped like a turtle shell, meant for one crew member who turned a hand crank to move it. It rose only a short distance and moved quite slowly. Still, that craft, called the Turtle, proved a small, hidden boat could work during battle in 1776.

A submarine operates through a fairly simple principle rooted in physics, namely buoyancy. Ballast tanks let water flood in, and the added weight pulls the craft downward toward the seabed. Compressed air forces that water back out through a narrow vent, and the lighter craft rises toward the surface, completing the cycle.

Later, an inventor named John Holland gave submarines a sleeker, far more practical shape, and navies around the world soon adopted this improved design for their fleets.

In 1958, a crew aboard the nuclear submarine USS Nautilus traveled deep beneath the Arctic ice, reaching the North Pole after staying submerged for a long, record-breaking stretch of time.

Today, scientists use advanced submarines to explore remote ocean trenches, study strange sea creatures, and locate old shipwrecks resting on the distant sea floor, adding greatly to our understanding of the deep ocean.

versions.text:
Picture a submarine at its dock near the busy harbor, its crew already aboard and its hatches sealed, waiting to slip beneath the waves at the start of a long voyage across open, unpredictable water far from any shore.

Long before modern navies, a man in England named Cornelius Drebbel built a boat that could travel beneath the sea, at a time when few people believed such a craft could possibly work at all. He packed it with wood and tough, carefully stitched leather to keep the water out, and rowers inside moved it slowly with long oars, rising and sinking as the voyage required. It was tried first for amusement in front of curious crowds, and later inspired cruder weapons used in wars across medieval and early modern Europe.

Years later, an American inventor named David Bushnell envisioned a markedly different design, one meant for a surprise attack unseen beneath the water's surface during a time of open conflict. He painstakingly built a small craft shaped like a turtle shell, intended for one crew member who turned a hand crank to move it slowly through the water. It rose only a short distance and moved quite slowly, yet that craft, called the Turtle, conclusively proved that a small, hidden boat could operate effectively during battle in 1776, a lesson later engineers would not forget.

A submarine operates through a fairly simple principle rooted in physics, namely buoyancy, and mastering that single principle took centuries of careful trial and error. Ballast tanks let water flood in, and the added weight pulls the craft downward toward the seabed, while compressed air forces that same water back out through a narrow vent, letting the lighter craft rise toward the surface once again. This careful balancing act lets a modern crew hover at nearly any depth they choose.

Later, an inventor named John Holland gave submarines a sleeker, far more practical shape, equipped with both an engine for the surface and a separate motor for diving, and navies around the world soon adopted this improved design for their rapidly expanding fleets of warships.

In 1958, a crew aboard the nuclear submarine USS Nautilus traveled deep beneath the Arctic ice, reaching the North Pole after staying submerged for a long, record-breaking stretch of time without ever once surfacing for air, a feat that stunned naval experts everywhere.

Today, scientists use advanced submarines to explore remote ocean trenches, study strange and unfamiliar sea creatures, and locate old shipwrecks resting on the distant sea floor, adding considerably to our understanding of the deep ocean and its many enduring mysteries that still remain unsolved.

versions.title: Submarines: Exploring Under the Sea
versions.text:
Picture a submarine at its dock near the busy harbor, its crew already aboard and its hatches sealed tight, waiting to slip beneath the waves at the start of a long voyage across open, unpredictable water far from any familiar shore.

Long before modern navies, a man in England named Cornelius Drebbel built a boat that could travel beneath the sea, at a time when few people believed such a strange craft could possibly work at all. He packed it with wood and tough, carefully stitched leather to keep the water out, and rowers inside moved it slowly with long oars, rising and sinking as the voyage required. It was tried first for amusement in front of curious, skeptical crowds, and later inspired cruder weapons used in wars across medieval and early modern Europe alike.

Years later, an American inventor named David Bushnell envisioned a markedly different design, one meant for a surprise attack unseen beneath the water's dark surface during a time of open conflict. He painstakingly built a small craft shaped like a turtle shell, intended for one crew member who turned a hand crank to move it slowly through the water. It rose only a short distance and moved quite slowly, yet that craft, called the Turtle, conclusively proved that a small, hidden boat could operate effectively during battle in 1776, a lesson that later engineers would never forget.

A submarine operates through a fairly simple principle rooted in physics, namely buoyancy, and this same principle governs essentially every dive a submarine has ever made, from the earliest wooden hulls to the largest nuclear giants. Ballast tanks let water flood in, and the added weight pulls the craft downward toward the seabed, while compressed air forces that same water back out through a narrow vent, letting the lighter craft rise toward the surface once again. This careful balancing act lets a modern crew hover at nearly any depth they choose, for as long as their supplies allow.

Later, an inventor named John Holland gave submarines a sleeker, far more practical shape, equipped with both an engine for the surface and a separate motor for diving, and navies around the world soon adopted this improved design for their rapidly expanding fleets of warships.

In 1958, a crew aboard the nuclear submarine USS Nautilus traveled deep beneath the Arctic ice, reaching the North Pole after staying submerged for a long, record-breaking stretch of time without ever once surfacing for air, a feat that stunned naval experts around the entire world and reshaped what people believed submarines could ever accomplish.

Today, scientists use advanced submarines to explore remote ocean trenches, study strange and unfamiliar sea creatures, and locate old shipwrecks resting on the distant sea floor, adding considerably, year after year, to our understanding of the deep ocean and its many enduring mysteries that still remain entirely unsolved, even after more than a century of determined exploration.

MID.modelAnswer: Submarines changed enormously between the first rowing boat and today's vessels. The earliest underwater boat was made of wood and leather, and rowers moved it with long oars. Later, a small, turtle-shaped craft used a hand crank and proved that a hidden underwater craft could work in battle. Over time, inventors gave submarines a sleeker design, and navies adopted these improvements for their fleets. These details show that submarines slowly grew from a simple rowing craft into far more capable vessels.

HIGH.prompt: Some people argue that the invention of the nuclear submarine is the most important advance in submarine history. Do you agree or disagree? Support your position with evidence from the article.
checklist: I supported it with at least two pieces of evidence from the article.
I explained how my evidence supports my position.
HIGH.modelAnswer: I agree that the nuclear submarine represents the most important advance in submarine history, because it transformed what these vessels could achieve. The article explains that the USS Nautilus stayed submerged beneath the Arctic ice for a long, record-breaking stretch of time, reaching the North Pole without surfacing, something earlier submarines like Bushnell's Turtle could never have attempted. This achievement built on centuries of earlier progress, from Drebbel's simple rowing craft to Holland's sleeker design, but nuclear power finally freed submarines from needing to surface frequently. That new freedom is why I consider the nuclear submarine the most transformative step in this long history.
